questions.question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs, with the largest value moving to the end each pass?
questions.rationale: Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; after each full pass the largest remaining value has bubbled to the end of the list.

questions.question: In the worked example, sorting 5 3 8 1 4 with bubble sort left the list as which state after pass 2?
questions.rationale: The pass table shows pass 1 ending at 3 5 1 4 8 and pass 2 (two swaps) ending at 3 1 4 5 8.

questions.question: What is merge sort's worst-case running time?
questions.rationale: Merge sort runs in O(n log n) on every input — best, average, and worst — because the split tree has log₂ n levels, each costing O(n) to merge.

questions.question: Why is merge sort not in-place?
options: Merging needs an O(n) scratch buffer
It keeps a log of all swaps
questions.rationale: In-place means O(1) extra memory; merge sort needs an O(n) buffer while merging the sorted halves.

questions.question: Which scenario degrades quicksort to its O(n²) worst case?
options: A bad pivot such as the first element of already-sorted input
Using extra memory for a buffer
questions.rationale: Quicksort is usually fastest in practice, but a bad pivot on sorted input partitions extremely unevenly, giving quadratic time.

questions.question: How does counting sort beat the Ω(n log n) comparison lower bound?
options: By using keys directly as array indices
By sorting only half the list
questions.rationale: Non-comparison sorts use keys as array indices: counting sort tallies occurrences and rebuilds in order, running in O(n + k) for key range k.

questions.question: Which pair of sorts does the master table list as stable AND in-place in O(1) extra space?
questions.rationale: Bubble and insertion sorts are both stable with O(1) extra space; merge needs O(n) space, while quick and heap are not stable.

questions.question: For a tiny array of about ten nearly-sorted items, which sort does the lesson recommend?
questions.rationale: Insertion sort is adaptive — nearly-sorted input finishes in O(n) — and wins on constants for tiny arrays, which is why libraries call it for short runs.

questions.question: What are Timsort and introsort, as shipped by Python/Java and C++?
options: A stable merge/insertion hybrid and a quicksort that turns to heapsort
Variants of selection sort for GPUs
questions.rationale: Timsort is a stable merge/insertion hybrid running in O(n) on nearly-sorted data; introsort is quicksort that switches to heapsort when recursion runs deep.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why does sorted data matter so much?
options: Binary search needs it, dropping lookups from O(n) to O(log n)
It removes the need for memory
questions.rationale: Sorted input enables binary search at O(log n), collapses duplicates into adjacent runs for one-scan dedup, and puts medians at a known index.
